“The doctors believe it is advisable to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to remove it,” he said. “The operation is already scheduled for the next few days.”

VATICAN CITY >> Pope Leo said on Sunday that doctors had detected a small growth on his lung during a recent health check and he would be undergoing surgery this week to remove it, in the first health scare of the 71-year-old pontiff’s tenure.
Leo told pilgrims in St. Peter’s Square for his weekly Sunday prayer that the growth, a small nodule, was “well-contained” and had been spotted early.
The Vatican did not say whether the nodule is believed to be malignant.
“Recently, during some medical examinations, doctors found a localized nodule in my lung,” said the pontiff. “It was detected at a very early stage and is well contained.”
“The doctors believe it is advisable to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to remove it,” he said. “The operation is already scheduled for the next few days.”
A nodule on the lung is a small, localised lesion that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than 5% of lung nodules overall prove cancerous, although risk rises with age, size, and other factors such as smoking.

sources.text: By — Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press By — Colleen Barry, Associated Press Colleen Barry, Associated Press Leave your feedback Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/pope-leo-to-undergo-surgery-to-remove-nodule-on-his-lung Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Pope Leo to undergo surgery to remove nodule on his lung World Oct 11, 2026 2:34 PM EDT VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday he will undergo surgery "in the coming days" to remove a nodule on his lung, in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The 71-year-old Leo said the nodule was found at an early stage and was "circumscribed" or small and well-localized. The Vatican said Leo's expected recovery time from surgery would be a week. The American pope made the announcement during his Sunday noon blessing in an unusual display of transparency about his health. He thanked the crowd for their closeness and entrusted himself to their prayers. The Vatican didn't say exactly when the surgery would take place, other than in the early days of this week. Leo has one upcoming main event: the closing Mass on Wednesday of a weeklong conference on family ministry, but Vatican officials suggested he might miss it. A nodule can be benign or malignant A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (1 inch) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening. "Lung nodules are fairly common and are often benign, but benign and cancerous nodules can have a similar appearance on imaging," said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown's Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center. "When there is sufficient concern, and when it is safe to do so based on the location of the nodule and the overall health of the patient, surgical removal can provide a definitive diagnosis," he said. A statue of the late Pope John Paul II outside the entrance to Gemelli Hospital, where Pope Leo is expected to undergo surgery this week to remove a small growth on his lung, in Rome, Italy, October 11, 2026. Photo by Matteo Minnella/Reuters. If the nodule turns out to be cancerous, the prognosis is "excellent" since it will have been removed at an early stage and surgery alone might be all Leo needs in terms of treatment, he said in an interview. "It often can be a blessing in disguise to remove that cancer before it has a chance to grow or to spread," he said. Leo has no previously known health problems and is physically active, with weekly tennis matches and swimming at the papal summer retreat in Castel Gandolfo. The pope has a major trip planned Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear how or whether the planned surgery and recovery might affect the itinerary, but Leo said earlier in his remarks Sunday that he still planned to go. In his remarks, delivered in Italian, Leo said that during a recent medical check, "doctors found a circumscribed nodule in my lung. It was detected at a very early stage and is well-localized. The doctors believe it's best to take action, so, following their advice, I have decided to have surgery to remove it." He thanked the faithful "for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers." Surgery to be at the pope's hospital Leo's predecessor, Pope Francis, died April 21, 2025, of a stroke following a long hospitalization brought on by a respiratory crisis that developed into double pneumonia. Francis suffered from chronic lung disease and had part of one lung removed as a young man. Francis' illnesses were characterized by a dizzying and sometimes problematic release of information from the Vatican, which always closely guards the privacy of a pope's health. In one infamous incident, the Vatican said Francis had gone to the hospital in March 2023 for scheduled tests, but the pontiff later revealed he had felt pain in his chest and was rushed to the hospital where bronchitis was diagnosed. He ended up being admitted for three days. This time around, Leo appeared keen to control the message and deliver it himself, using one of his most public encounters with the faithful to alert them of his condition and impending hospital stay. Leo is expected to undergo surgery at Rome's Gemelli hospital, where Francis and popes before him were treated and where there is a special apartment for pontiffs. On Sunday, there was no obvious sign that the pope had already been admitted. A nodule doesn't mean cancer but should be investigated Dr. Dionysis Papadatos-Pastos, an oncologist and lung cancer specialist at The London Clinic, stressed that an incidental finding of a lung nodule doesn't mean lung cancer. And in fact "a well-circumscribed nodule does suggest that this is less likely to be cancer." But he said cancer was possible and the main imperative is to investigate. "The worst thing you can do is ignore a lung nodule," he said in an interview. Liu, the Georgetown oncologist, said surgical removal in such a case was standard, especially for someone in otherwise good health and if the nodule is in an easily accessible location. A needle biopsy on a lung nodule can be difficult and may not provide doctors with enough information, he said. "In these cases, surgery itself, while it may seem dramatic, is often very safe, very straightforward with a rapid recovery," he said, adding that Leo should be in good shape to travel to Latin America barring any complications. Leo is not known to be a smoker. Liu noted that 1 in 5 people diagnosed with lung cancer have no history of smoking. Dr. Massimo Di Maio, president of the Italian Association of Medical Oncology, said it will be important to determine if the nodule is benign or malignant, and if it is malignant, whether it has spread. When the disease is detected at an early stage "the aim … is curative," he added. Depending on what is found, possible treatments can include chemotherapy and radiation therapy, Di Maio told Italy's private Sky TG24. "When we talk about something being localized, that can also refer to the need to establish whether the disease is confined to that one site or whether scans show signs of disease elsewhere," he said, adding that he has not treated the pope and was speaking about the disease in general. "Being physically fit and healthy is certainly an important starting point for coping as well as possible with treatment, including surgery," he added. Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni, among the few outsiders to visit Francis during his long final hospitalization, expressed her support, and that of the Italian government, for Leo "as he faces this challenge in the coming days." In a statement, she added that "the serenity and calm with which he spoke about it" were reassuring. Barry reported from Milan; AP reporter Danica Kirka contributed from London. Pope Leo XIV faces his first major health concern since becoming head of the Catholic Church, with a medical procedure scheduled for later this week. The 71-year-old has offered reassurance about his condition, although questions remain about the nature of the abnormality doctors discovered.
His immediate schedule includes a major Mass and a public prayer, but the Vatican has not yet clarified whether he will attend either event.
Pope Leo XIV Reveals Doctors Found Growth On Lung
Pope Leo has revealed that he will undergo surgery after doctors discovered a small growth on his lung during a recent medical examination. The pontiff shared the news on Sunday, October 11, while addressing pilgrims gathered in St. Peter’s Square for his weekly prayer.
According to Reuters, Leo assured the crowd that doctors detected the growth early and that it appeared to be contained. “Recently, during some medical examinations, doctors found a localized nodule in my lung,” he explained.
The pope said he had accepted his doctors’ recommendation to remove the growth, with the operation scheduled for the coming days. The Vatican expects Leo to spend approximately one week recovering from the procedure. However, officials have not disclosed whether the nodule is cancerous.
The announcement marks the first publicly known health concern of Leo’s papacy since his election in May 2025.
How The Surgery Could Disrupt Vatican Schedule
Pope Leo’s upcoming medical procedure could disrupt several engagements already on the Vatican’s calendar. According to an official Vatican notice, the pontiff is scheduled to preside over a Eucharistic celebration outside St. Peter’s Basilica on Wednesday, October 14, at 10 a.m.
The Mass will mark the conclusion of a meeting celebrating the tenth anniversary of “Amoris Laetitia,” an apostolic exhortation on family life. The event is expected to bring together senior Catholic clergy, including cardinals, archbishops, and bishops.
Another public engagement is listed for Sunday, October 18, when Leo is set to lead the traditional Angelus prayer at noon in St. Peter’s Square. Both appearances fall within the period when the pontiff is expected to be undergoing treatment or recovering.
However, the Vatican has not yet announced whether it will cancel, postpone, or handle either engagement differently.

The Argentine pontiff also struggled with chronic knee pain and sciatica, eventually relying on a wheelchair for many public appearances.
His most serious health crisis arrived in February 2025, when he was hospitalized with a respiratory infection that developed into double pneumonia. Francis spent 38 days at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital receiving treatment before returning to the Vatican. He died on April 21, 2025, at age 88, after suffering a stroke.

Watch: Pope Leo XIV Shares He Will Undergo Surgery to Remove Nodule in His Lung
Pope Leo XIV is sharing insight into his physical health.
Indeed, the religious leader, born Robert Francis Prevost, shared during the Sunday Angelus prayer in Rome, Italy, Oct. 11 that he is set to undergo surgery to remove a nodule in one of his lungs.
“Dear friends, during some recent medical examinations, the doctors found a small, localized nodule in my lung,” Pope Leo told those gathered in St Peter’s Square, per a news release shared by the Vatican. “It was detected at a very early stage and is well-localized. The doctors believe that it is best to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to remove it.”
“The operation is already scheduled to take place in the coming days,” he added. “I thank you for your spiritual closeness and entrust myself to your prayers. Thank you, and happy Sunday!”
The Director of the Holy See Press Office Matteo Bruni also shared in a statement that the operation, which is set to take place at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, “is scheduled for the first days of this week and the estimated post-operative recovery time will be about one week."
Lung nodules are a common condition formed from small clumps of cells in the lungs, according to Mayo Clinic. And while most lung nodules are scar tissue from past lung infections, they don’t typically cause any symptoms. Rather, “They're often found by accident on a chest X-ray or CT scan done for some other reason.”

sources.news_title: Pope Leo XIV to undergo surgery to remove a nodule on his lung
sources.text:
VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday he will undergo surgery “in the coming days” to remove a nodule on his lung, in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate.
The 71-year-old Leo said the nodule was found at an early stage and was “circumscribed” or well-localized. The Vatican said Leo's expected recovery time from surgery would be a week.
The American pope made the announcement during his Sunday noon blessing. He thanked the crowd for their closeness and entrusted himself to their prayers.
The Vatican didn’t say exactly when the surgery would take place, other than in the early days of this week. Leo has one upcoming main event: the closing Mass on Wednesday of a weeklong conference on family ministry, but Vatican officials suggested he might miss it.
A nodule can be benign or malignant
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (1 inch) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening.
“Lung nodules are fairly common and are often benign, but benign and cancerous nodules can have a similar appearance on imaging," said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center.
"When there is sufficient concern, and when it is safe to do so based on the location of the nodule and the overall health of the patient, surgical removal can provide a definitive diagnosis,” he said.
If the nodule turns out to be cancerous, the prognosis is “excellent” since it will have been removed at an early stage and surgery alone might be all Leo needs in terms of treatment, he said in an interview.
"It often can be a blessing in disguise to remove that cancer before it has a chance to grow or to spread,” he said.
Leo has no previously known health problems and is physically active, with weekly tennis matches and swimming at the papal summer retreat in Castel Gandolfo.
The pope has a major trip planned Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear how or whether the planned surgery and recovery might affect the itinerary, but Leo said earlier in his remarks Sunday that he still planned to go.
In his remarks, delivered in Italian, Leo said that during a recent medical check, “doctors found a small, localized nodule in my lung. It was detected at a very early stage and is circumscribed. The doctors believe it’s best to take action, so, following their advice, I have decided to have surgery to remove it."
He thanked the faithful "for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers.”
Surgery to be at the pope's hospital
Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, died April 21, 2025, of a stroke following a long hospitalization brought on by a respiratory crisis that developed into double pneumonia. Francis suffered from chronic lung disease and had part of one lung removed as a young man.
Leo is expected to undergo surgery at Rome's Gemelli hospital, where Francis and popes before him were treated and where there is a special apartment for pontiffs. On Sunday, there was no obvious sign that the pope had already been admitted.
Dr. Dionysis Papadatos-Pastos, an oncologist and lung cancer specialist at The London Clinic, stressed that an incidental finding of a lung nodule doesn't mean lung cancer. And in fact “a well-circumscribed nodule does suggest that this is less likely to be cancer."
But he said cancer was possible and the main imperative is to investigate. "The worst thing you can do is ignore a lung nodule,” he said in an interview.
Liu, the Georgetown oncologist, said surgical removal in such a case was standard, especially for someone in otherwise good health and if the nodule is in an easily accessible location. A needle biopsy on a lung nodule can be difficult and may not provide doctors with enough information, he said.
"In these cases, surgery itself, while it may seem dramatic, is often very safe, very straightforward with a rapid recovery,” he said, adding that Leo should be in good shape to travel to Latin America barring any complications.
Dr. Massimo Di Maio, president of the Italian Association of Medical Oncology, said it will be important to determine if the nodule is benign or malignant, and if it is malignant, whether it has spread. When the disease is detected at an early stage “the aim … is curative,” he added.
Depending on what is found, possible treatments can include chemotherapy and radiation therapy, Di Maio told Italy’s private Sky TG24.
“When we talk about something being localized, that can also refer to the need to establish whether the disease is confined to that one site or whether scans show signs of disease elsewhere,” he said, adding that he has not treated the pope and was speaking about the disease in general.
“Being physically fit and healthy is certainly an important starting point for coping as well as possible with treatment, including surgery,” he added.
Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni, among the few outsiders to visit Francis during his long final hospitalization, expressed her support, and that of the Italian government, for Leo “as he faces this challenge in the coming days.” In a statement, she added that “the serenity and calm with which he spoke about it” were reassuring.

Pope Leo XIV is planning to undergo surgery to remove a recently discovered lung nodule.

“Recently, during some medical examinations, doctors discovered a well-defined lung nodule, detected at a very early stage and clearly localised,” the Pope told worshippers.
“The doctors consider it appropriate to intervene, and so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to have it removed.”

Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said the expected postoperative hospital stay would be approximately one week. Officials have not publicly identified a precise date for the procedure or provided additional clinical details concerning the nodule.
The announcement was also reported by GB News, which described the intervention as emergency surgery following the discovery of the localized growth.
However, the Vatican has characterized the operation as a scheduled procedure recommended by physicians rather than an emergency intervention performed in response to an immediate medical crisis. The distinction is important because the pontiff has not been reported to be experiencing acute respiratory distress or other symptoms requiring urgent hospitalization.
Leo emphasized that the growth had been identified early and appeared confined to a specific area of the lung. His remarks did not establish whether the nodule is benign or malignant, and Vatican officials have not announced a cancer diagnosis.
A pulmonary nodule is a relatively small area of abnormal tissue that may be detected during medical imaging. Such growths can develop for several reasons, including previous infections, inflammation, scar tissue or tumors. Many are noncancerous, although medical evaluation is necessary to determine their significance.
The decision to remove a nodule surgically can depend on its size, appearance, location, growth pattern and the patient’s medical history. Physicians may recommend surgery when they consider removal appropriate for diagnosis, treatment or prevention of further complications.
In Leo’s case, the Vatican has not disclosed the imaging findings, the size of the growth or whether a biopsy was performed before the decision to operate. There has also been no announcement concerning the exact surgical technique or whether additional treatment might be required.
The American Cancer Society explains that many lung nodules are discovered incidentally during imaging performed for unrelated medical reasons. While some require monitoring or further examination, others may warrant removal depending on their characteristics.
The Pope’s disclosure drew attention because he has generally maintained a demanding schedule since his election in May 2025. Leo, the first American-born pontiff, has continued presiding over major liturgical celebrations, meeting international leaders and receiving visitors at the Vatican.
Born Robert Francis Prevost in Chicago on Sept. 14, 1955, Leo was elected to succeed Pope Francis following the latter’s death in April 2025. His election brought an American to the papacy for the first time in the Catholic Church’s history.

His appeals concerning Ukraine have formed part of the Holy See’s broader efforts to promote negotiations and support communities affected by the war.

The U.S. Defense Department has announced plans for Hasan’s execution by firing squad on Dec. 3, with officials also proposing that the procedure be livestreamed. The announcement prompted criticism from Catholic leaders and renewed debate over the use of capital punishment in the United States.

The Pope’s intervention occurred shortly before his medical announcement, placing two separate developments involving his leadership at the center of international attention.

For now, the Holy See’s public statements indicate that the Pope has accepted his doctors’ recommendation for early surgical intervention and is expected to remain hospitalized for approximately one week.
The announcement marks the first significant health-related interruption anticipated during his pontificate, coming less than two years after he assumed leadership of the Catholic Church.
Leo’s immediate priority will be the removal of the lung nodule and recovery at Gemelli Hospital. Pope Leo XIV told pilgrims gathered for his Sunday noon blessing that he will undergo surgery in the coming days for a nodular lesion in his lung, an announcement that lands just weeks before his first planned trip to Latin America as pontiff. The 71-year-old, born Robert Francis Prevost in Chicago and raised in south suburban Dolton, said the lesion was found at an early stage and was circumscribed, and he asked for prayers, especially for his upcoming trip to Peru.
According to FOX 32 Chicago, which cited reporting from the Associated Press, Pope Leo XIV is expected to be hospitalized at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, where he is expected to receive treatment in a special apartment reserved for the pope. Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said the pope would be hospitalized in the first days of the week, with a recovery period expected to last about one week. The Vatican released no further details immediately, and officials have not said what impact the surgery or recovery will have on the pope's planned Nov. 7–16 trip to Latin America.
Pope Leo XIV has no previously known health problems, the outlet's report notes, and he has kept up an active routine that includes weekly tennis games and swims at the papal summer retreat in Castel Gandolfo. The timing of the surgery, just weeks before his scheduled departure for Latin America, has left the fate of that itinerary an open question.
Why the Peru Leg Carries Extra Weight
The uncertainty around the November trip resonates especially in Peru, where Prevost spent decades as an Augustinian missionary before rising through the Church's ranks. He began his missionary work in the northern town of Chulucanas in 1985 and later served as Bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, acquiring Peruvian citizenship that same year, according to the Diocese of Joliet. Those pastoral roots run deeper in Peru than almost anywhere else he has served, which is part of why his planned stop there has drawn close attention even before the surgery announcement.
Before his election, Prevost also spent two consecutive six-year terms as Prior General of the worldwide Order of Saint Augustine from 2001 to 2013, per the Augustinian Province of Saint Thomas of Villanova. The order had members in more than 40 countries and every continent. He had earlier led the Chicago Augustinians as Provincial Prior from 1998 to 2001, and in January 2023 Pope Francis appointed him Prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops and President of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America, a post in which he vetted bishop candidates worldwide, as America Magazine reported at the time.
A Papal Suite With a Long History
Gemelli Hospital's 10th-floor papal suite has hosted pontiffs through major medical episodes for decades. St. John Paul II spent 153 days there across nine separate admissions and reportedly nicknamed the suite “Vatican III,” according to AP News. The suite has a private chapel reserved for popes. Pope Francis was also treated there multiple times during his pontificate, including a 10-day hospitalization in 2021 for colon surgery, a nine-day stay in 2023 for abdominal hernia repair, and an 18-day stay earlier in 2025 for double pneumonia. Pope Benedict XVI, by contrast, was never hospitalized at Gemelli during his papacy, the same AP report notes.
Pope Leo XIV's election on May 8, 2025, made him the 267th leader of the Roman Catholic Church, the first U.S.-born pontiff, and the first Augustinian friar to hold the papacy, succeeding Pope Francis after a two-day conclave, according to the National Catholic Reporter. The milestone made the surgery announcement resonate well beyond Rome, touching off concern in both Chicago and Peru, the two places that shaped his life before the papacy.
Dolton's Pope Keeps His Hometown Close
Dolton's Pope Keeps His Hometown Close In Chicago, Pope Leo XIV's ties to Dolton have only deepened since his election. The Village Board there officially designated his boyhood home at 212 E. 141st Place as a local historic landmark in December 2025, months after the village purchased the three-bedroom brick house for $375,000 to turn it into a historic and tourist site. The home is tied to the Prevost family's Dolton roots.
His connection to the city has also played out through his lifelong fandom of the Chicago White Sox. On September 29, ahead of the team's playoff opener, the White Sox received a personal letter from the pope addressed to chairman Jerry Reinsdorf, offering blessings and describing sports as a “school of life,” as Hoodline reported on September 30. That came weeks after the team's Pope Hat Night in August, when more than 38,000 hats were distributed for a sellout crowd.
Pope Leo XIV also graduated from Villanova University in 1977 with a Bachelor of Science degree in mathematics, Villanova University said. For now, the Vatican has offered no further details beyond the surgery timeline and the pope's own request for prayers, leaving the question of his Peru trip unresolved as he prepares for the procedure this week.
